# Detections

<!-- Generated by `dayag rules --markdown`. Do not edit by hand. -->

Every finding Dayag can report. Points add up to the score (0-100), counting each rule once however many times it fires. Rules marked 🌐 only run with `--online`.

| Verdict | Score |
| --- | --- |
| Malicious | 70-100 |
| Likely phishing | 40-69 |
| Suspicious | 15-39 |
| No strong indicators | 0-14 |

## Authentication

| ID | Finding | Severity | Points | ATT&CK | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `AUTH-DMARC-FAIL` | DMARC failed | high | +30 | [T1566](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/) | Neither SPF nor DKIM passed in alignment with the From domain. This is what a forged From address looks like. |
| `AUTH-COMPAUTH-FAIL` | Microsoft composite authentication failed | high | +30 | [T1566](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/) | Exchange Online combined SPF, DKIM, DMARC and its own reputation data and concluded that the sender is not who it claims to be. |
| `AUTH-FORGED-RESULTS` | Forged authentication header | medium | +15 | [T1566](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/) | An Authentication-Results header lower in the message claims a pass that the receiving server did not report. Senders can add any header they like, so only the topmost results, written by the receiving server, are trusted. |
| `AUTH-SPF-FAIL` | SPF failed | medium | +15 | [T1566](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/) | The server that delivered the email is not allowed to send for the envelope sender's domain. Alone it can be a misconfigured forwarder; with a DMARC failure it means the sender is forged. |
| `AUTH-SPF-SOFTFAIL` | SPF soft-failed | low | +5 |  | The envelope sender's domain says this server is probably not one of its own. |
| `AUTH-SPF-NONE` | No usable SPF result | low | +5 |  | The envelope sender's domain publishes no SPF record, or it could not be evaluated. |
| `AUTH-DKIM-FAIL` | DKIM signature failed | low | +5 |  | The message carries a signature that does not verify: it was changed in transit or the signature is fake. |
| `AUTH-DKIM-NONE` | Not DKIM-signed | low | +5 |  | Legitimate bulk and corporate senders almost always sign their mail. |
| `AUTH-DMARC-NONE` | From domain has no DMARC policy | low | +5 |  | Without a DMARC policy, receivers have no instruction to reject mail that forges the domain. |
| `AUTH-DKIM-UNALIGNED` | Signed by a different domain | info | +0 |  | The DKIM signature belongs to another domain, usually an email service provider. Common and legitimate, but worth knowing when the From domain matters. |
| `AUTH-DMARC-PASS` | DMARC passed | info | -10 |  | The email really comes from the From domain. That proves where it came from, not that the domain is trustworthy: attackers authenticate their own lookalike domains too. |
| `AUTH-MISSING` | No authentication results | info | +0 |  | The receiving server's verdicts are missing, so SPF, DKIM and DMARC cannot be judged. Export the original message with full headers if possible. |

## Sender

| ID | Finding | Severity | Points | ATT&CK | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `SENDER-LOOKALIKE` | Sender domain imitates a brand | critical | +50 | [T1583.001](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583/001/), [T1656](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1656/) | The From or Reply-To domain is a homoglyph, character swap, typo or TLD swap of a well-known brand's domain. |
| `SENDER-COMBOSQUAT` | Sender domain contains a brand name | high | +30 | [T1583.001](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583/001/), [T1656](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1656/) | A brand name combined with other words (paypal-support.com) is the most common way to register a convincing phishing domain. |
| `SENDER-DISPLAY-BRAND` | Display name impersonates a brand | high | +30 | [T1656](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1656/) | The display name claims to be a brand, but the address does not belong to it. Most mail apps show only the display name. |
| `SENDER-DISPLAY-ADDRESS` | Display name contains a different address | high | +30 | [T1656](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1656/) | A display name such as "security@bank.com" hides the real sender address in clients that only show names. |
| `SENDER-REPLYTO-FREEMAIL` | Replies go to a free email account | high | +25 | [T1585.002](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1585/002/), [T1656](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1656/) | Answers are diverted to a webmail account the attacker controls: the signature move of business email compromise. |
| `SENDER-REPLYTO-MISMATCH` | Replies go to a different domain | medium | +15 |  | The Reply-To domain differs from the From domain, so a reply would reach someone other than the apparent sender. |
| `SENDER-FREEMAIL` | Sent from a free email account | low | +5 | [T1585.002](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1585/002/) | Anyone can create a free webmail account under any name. |
| `SENDER-RETURNPATH-MISMATCH` | Envelope sender differs from From | info | +0 |  | Bounces go to another domain. Normal for email service providers, so it only adds context. |
| `SENDER-NEW-DOMAIN` | Sender domain was registered recently 🌐 | high | +30 | [T1583.001](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583/001/) | Phishing domains are typically used within days of registration. |
| `SENDER-NO-MX` | Sender domain cannot receive email 🌐 | medium | +15 |  | The domain has no mail server, a sign of a throwaway domain set up only to send. |
| `SENDER-NO-DMARC` | Sender domain publishes no DMARC record 🌐 | info | +0 |  | Live DNS shows no DMARC record, so the domain can be spoofed freely. |

## Links

| ID | Finding | Severity | Points | ATT&CK | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `LINK-LOOKALIKE` | Link to a lookalike domain | critical | +50 | [T1566.002](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/002/), [T1583.001](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583/001/) | A link points to a homoglyph, character swap, typo or TLD swap of a well-known brand's domain. |
| `LINK-COMBOSQUAT` | Link domain contains a brand name | high | +30 | [T1566.002](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/002/), [T1583.001](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583/001/) | The link's domain uses a brand name it does not belong to. |
| `LINK-TEXT-MISMATCH` | Link text hides the real destination | high | +30 | [T1566.002](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/002/) | The visible link text shows one domain while the link goes to another. |
| `LINK-IP` | Link to a bare IP address | high | +30 | [T1566.002](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/002/) | Legitimate services use domain names. Raw IPs are typical of compromised or throwaway servers. |
| `LINK-USERINFO` | Link uses the @ trick | high | +30 | [T1566.002](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/002/) | In https://bank.com@evil.example/ everything before the @ is a user name and is ignored: the browser goes to evil.example. |
| `LINK-SCRIPT-SCHEME` | javascript: or data: link | high | +30 | [T1566.002](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/002/) | These links run code or open a page embedded in the link itself, bypassing URL filtering. |
| `LINK-IPFS` | Link to an IPFS gateway | high | +30 | [T1566.002](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/002/), [T1583.006](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583/006/) | Phishing kits are hosted on IPFS because content there is hard to take down. |
| `LINK-PUNYCODE` | Internationalised (punycode) domain | medium | +15 | [T1566.002](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/002/) | Non-Latin characters can make a domain look identical to another one. |
| `LINK-SHORTENER` | Shortened link hides the destination | medium | +15 | [T1566.002](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/002/) | The real destination is only revealed after clicking. |
| `LINK-FREE-HOSTING` | Link to a free hosting service | medium | +15 | [T1583.006](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583/006/) | Free hosting and file-sharing platforms let attackers put a phishing page on a reputable domain within minutes. |
| `LINK-CREDENTIAL-PATH` | Login-themed link to an unrelated site | low | +5 | [T1566.002](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/002/) | The link's path talks about logging in or verifying an account, on a domain that is neither the sender's nor a known brand's. |
| `LINK-RISKY-TLD` | Link to a frequently abused TLD | low | +5 |  | Some cheap top-level domains host a disproportionate share of phishing. |
| `LINK-NONSTANDARD-PORT` | Link uses an unusual port | low | +5 |  | Web servers on unusual ports are rare for legitimate services. |
| `LINK-NEW-DOMAIN` | Link domain was registered recently 🌐 | high | +25 | [T1583.001](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583/001/) | Phishing pages are typically hosted on domains only days old. |
| `LINK-REPUTATION` | URL or domain flagged by VirusTotal 🌐 | critical | +50 | [T1566.002](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/002/) | Several security vendors already classify a URL or domain in this email as malicious. |

## Attachments

| ID | Finding | Severity | Points | ATT&CK | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ATT-EXECUTABLE` | Executable or script attachment | critical | +50 | [T1566.001](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/), [T1204.002](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/) | The attachment runs code when opened. |
| `ATT-DOUBLE-EXT` | Double file extension | critical | +50 | [T1036.007](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1036/007/) | invoice.pdf.exe looks like a PDF when Windows hides known extensions. |
| `ATT-RTLO` | Right-to-left override in file name | critical | +50 | [T1036.002](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1036/002/) | An invisible Unicode control character reverses the end of the name, so 'invoice[U+202E]fdp.exe' is displayed as 'invoiceexe.pdf'. |
| `ATT-HTML-SMUGGLING` | HTML smuggling | critical | +50 | [T1027.006](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/006/) | The HTML file builds a file inside the browser from embedded data and offers it as a download, so the payload never crosses the mail gateway as a file. |
| `ATT-ARCHIVE-RISKY` | Archive contains executable content | critical | +50 | [T1566.001](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/), [T1204.002](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/) | The archive holds executables, scripts, shortcuts or disguised file names. |
| `ATT-TYPE-MISMATCH` | File content does not match its extension | high | +30 | [T1036.008](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1036/008/) | The file's real format, read from its first bytes, differs from what its name claims. |
| `ATT-HTML` | HTML or SVG attachment | high | +30 | [T1566.001](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/) | Local HTML files are used for credential-harvesting pages that load without any URL for filters to block. |
| `ATT-ENCRYPTED-ARCHIVE` | Password-protected archive | high | +30 | [T1027.013](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/013/) | Encryption stops the mail gateway from scanning the contents; the password is usually in the email body. |
| `ATT-DISK-IMAGE` | Disk image attachment | high | +30 | [T1553.005](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1553/005/) | Files inside ISO, IMG and VHD images do not inherit the Mark of the Web, so Windows skips its warnings. |
| `ATT-MACRO` | Office document with macros | high | +30 | [T1566.001](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/), [T1059.005](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/005/) | VBA macros are a classic first stage for malware. |
| `ATT-REMOTE-TEMPLATE` | Document loads remote content | high | +30 | [T1221](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1221/) | The document fetches a template or object from the internet when opened, a way to deliver macros or exploits after the file has passed scanning. |
| `ATT-ONENOTE` | OneNote attachment | high | +30 | [T1566.001](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/), [T1204.002](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/) | OneNote files can embed scripts behind fake 'click to view' buttons. |
| `ATT-PDF-ACTIVE` | PDF with active content | high | +30 | [T1566.001](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/), [T1204.002](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/) | The PDF contains JavaScript, launch actions, embedded files or rich media. |
| `ATT-REPUTATION` | Attachment flagged by VirusTotal 🌐 | critical | +50 | [T1566.001](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/) | Several security vendors already detect this exact file as malicious. |

## Content

| ID | Finding | Severity | Points | ATT&CK | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `CONTENT-PASSWORD-FIELD` | Email asks for a password directly | critical | +50 | [T1566](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/), [T1056.003](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1056/003/) | The email body contains a password field. No legitimate service collects passwords inside an email. |
| `CONTENT-FORM` | Email contains a form | high | +30 | [T1566](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/) | Forms inside an email send whatever the reader types straight to the attacker. |
| `CONTENT-GIFT-CARD` | Gift card request | high | +30 | [T1657](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1657/) | Requests to buy gift cards are a hallmark of CEO fraud: they are untraceable and instantly cashable. |
| `CONTENT-SCRIPT` | Email body contains scripts | medium | +15 | [T1566](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/) | Mail clients do not run scripts, so legitimate senders do not include them. |
| `CONTENT-PAYMENT` | Payment or bank-detail request | medium | +15 | [T1657](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1657/) | Asks to pay, transfer money or change bank details: the goal of business email compromise and fake-invoice fraud. |
| `CONTENT-CREDENTIALS` | Asks to sign in or verify an account | medium | +15 | [T1566](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/) | Credential phishing almost always asks the reader to log in, verify or update account details. |
| `CONTENT-FAKE-REPLY` | Fake reply or forward | medium | +15 | [T1566](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/) | The subject starts with RE: or FW: but the message is not part of any thread. Pretending to continue a conversation lowers the reader's guard. |
| `CONTENT-URGENCY` | Pressure and urgency | medium | +10 |  | Deadlines and threats push the reader to act before thinking. |
| `CONTENT-GENERIC-GREETING` | Generic greeting | low | +5 |  | Services you have an account with usually know your name. |
| `CONTENT-HIDDEN-TEXT` | Hidden text | low | +5 | [T1027](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/) | Large blocks of invisible text are used to confuse spam filters. |
| `CONTENT-IMAGE-ONLY` | Mostly images, little text | low | +5 | [T1566](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/) | Image-only emails hide their text from filters, and are how QR-code phishing (quishing) is delivered. |
| `CONTENT-TRACKING-PIXEL` | Tracking pixel | info | +0 |  | A 1x1 image tells the sender when the email is opened. Common in marketing, and the reason Dayag never loads remote images. |

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `INFRA-PHP-SCRIPT` | Sent by a script on a web server | medium | +15 | [T1584.004](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1584/004/) | The X-PHP-Originating-Script header shows the email was sent by a PHP script, often on a hacked website. |
